title: The report you can stand behind
subtitle: What must a report show before you put your name on it?
goal: After this lesson you can check a model report for six things (bound numbers, sizes and intervals, a baseline, wording that fits the evidence, segment results, first-page limits) and rewrite a sentence that fails.

predict.q: You catch a bug. Your assistant reruns the analysis and regenerates the HTML report. Where is a wrong number most likely to survive?
options: In the charts, because they are redrawn from scratch
In the sentences, where numbers typed around the first run stay put
In the appendix tables, which are the hardest part to rebuild
Nowhere: a rerun refreshes every number in the report
predict.reveal: In the sentences: a typed number stays put while the chart beside it moves, and the lesson shows how to make that impossible and what else a report has to carry.

segments.narration: Two reports on one yes-or-no model, the churn model you know. Same data, same test advertisers, both drafted by an assistant. The first is handsome: a gradient header, a bold headline, a confident summary. The second is plainer, and half a page longer. On Thursday one of them goes in front of the head of account management, and she will do what good stakeholders do: ask a question. Compared with what? How sure are you? So should we push tracking? The handsome report has nothing to say back. The plain one has already answered. The difference is not style. It is a short list of things you can check, and the same list fits any report: a spend forecast for finance, an invalid-traffic review.

visual.title: The report you can stand behind
visual.sub: Two reports, one model. Only one survives a question.

segments.narration: Start with the headline sentence. [[1]] The handsome report says the model identifies at-risk advertisers with high accuracy. Nothing in that can be checked. And accuracy is a strange boast, when predicting that nobody leaves is already about 87 percent accurate. [[2]] The plain report says this. Of the 200 advertisers the model ranked highest, 136 really churned. A random 200 would hold about 26. The interval on that count runs from 123 to 150, which is roughly how far it moves with the luck of who landed in the test months. And it names the rows: 4,000 advertisers from May and June that the model never saw. A count, a baseline beside it, an interval, and the rows. Every part can be checked.

left.label: Cannot be checked
left.sub: “The model identifies at-risk advertisers with high accuracy.”

right.label: Survives a question
right.sub: random 200: about 26 · 95% interval 123 to 150 · 4,000 unseen advertisers, May–June

segments.narration: Now the failure you will meet most often. Remember the leaked column that produced a perfect list: all 200 of the top 200 churned. Suppose you catch it after the report is drafted. The assistant reruns, and the chart now shows 136. The paragraph under the chart still celebrates 200. Nothing crashed. That sentence was typed once, around the first result, and only the chart was regenerated. The cure is mechanical. Every number in the prose is inserted by the script, from the same results file that feeds the charts. Nothing is typed. Then a rerun moves the sentence and the chart together, and the assistant can list every number in the text beside its source.

visual.title: Typed numbers go stale. Bound numbers cannot.
visual.code:
# Typed: survives the rerun, wrongly
summary = "All 200 of the top 200 churned."

# Bound: read from the checked results
r = results["top_200"]
summary = (f"Of the top {r['k']}, "
           f"{r['churners']} churned.")
visual.note: After the leak is fixed the results file says 136. Only the bound sentence follows it.

segments.narration: Next, the verbs. The handsome report says conversion tracking reduces churn by 11 points. Reduces is a claim about changing something, and evidence comes in four tiers. [[1]] Observed: two groups differed. That earns churned less, or is associated with. [[2]] Adjusted: the gap survives holding the visible columns fixed. Say it remains after adjusting. [[3]] Compared: the change in a group that got something, minus the change in a similar group without it. Module five's launch earns rose about 5 points more than the comparison group, assuming the two would have moved together. [[4]] Tested: a coin decided who got the change. Only this tier earns reduces. Tracking's true effect in this simulated world is about 2 points. On real data you cannot look it up, so the verb must carry the tier.

visual.title: The verb must match the evidence
rows: Two groups compared: 7.2% vs 18.4% churn, gap 11.2 pts
Visible columns held fixed: gap 6.5 pts
Change in the launch group minus change in a similar untreated group: +4.7 pts, interval 3.2 to 6.2
“rose 4.7 points more than the comparison group”; assumes the two would have moved together
A coin decided who got the change
visual.note: Row 3 is the module 5 launch; the other rows are conversion tracking, whose true effect in this simulated world is 2.3 pts. Knowable only because it is simulated.

segments.narration: The assistant drafts the prose as well, and its default register is confident. Hand it a bar chart and it writes a story. [[1]] Something like: gaming churn rose sharply in April, pointing to growing dissatisfaction in the vertical. Read that the way you would read its code. Sharply, against what? Dissatisfaction, measured where? [[2]] Underneath: 14 percent in March and 19 in April. Each month is about 250 advertisers. The interval on that difference runs from about minus 2 to plus 11 points. Zero is inside it. The dissatisfaction explains a rise that may not exist. Every comparison carries its group sizes and its interval, and the sentence may not say more than they do.

visual.title: Read the prose like the code

left.label: The assistant's sentence
left.sub: “Gaming churn rose sharply in April, pointing to growing dissatisfaction.”

right.label: What the numbers support
right.sub: 14.2% of 253 advertisers, then 19.1% of 246: within noise

segments.narration: Last, the first page. Two things go there. [[1]] One is a provenance line: when the data was pulled, which rows were in, which model version. Here: 6,000 advertisers from January to March to train, April left out, 4,000 from May and June to test. The other is a short paragraph on what the reader should not conclude. [[2]] This model ranks risk. It does not say why advertisers leave, or that a call would keep them. [[3]] Its percentages run low. [[4]] And it does not serve every size equally. The working list catches about 55 percent of small churners and about 25 percent of large ones, though large accounts are two thirds of the dollars lost. Limits in an appendix are limits nobody read.

visual.title: First page, before any chart
items: Provenance: pull date · train Jan–Mar 6,000 · April out · test May–Jun 4,000 · model version
Ranks risk. Not why they leave, nor who a call would keep
Top 400 catch 55% of small churners, 25% of large (two thirds of lost spend)

segments.narration: Brief and audit. The report is stage four, built only from checked numbers. Ask for six things, and look for each in the output. [[1]] Every number in the text read from the results file, with a list of where each came from. [[2]] Group sizes and an interval beside every comparison. [[3]] The baseline next to the model, at the same list size. [[4]] Each finding labelled observed, adjusted, compared or tested, with verbs to match. [[5]] Results by segment. [[6]] A first page with the provenance line and what not to conclude. Then read every sentence and ask which number on the page supports it. If none does, the sentence goes. A fresh assistant session, handed only the draft and told to list every unsupported sentence, makes a cheap second reader.

visual.title: Brief and audit: six things a report must show
rows: Where did that number come from?
Group sizes and an interval by each comparison
Compared with what? Rule 246 of 711, model 321
Wording that matches the evidence tier

segments.narration: So before your name goes on a report, run the six checks, and send back any sentence that claims more than its evidence. One lesson is left: the whole course folded into a path you can walk with a question you have never seen.

visual.title: The report you can stand behind
items: Every number traces back to a computed result
Every claim uses the words its evidence has earned
The limits are on the first page

takeaways: Every number in the text is read from a computed result and carries its baseline, group size, interval and rows.
The verb matches the evidence tier: observed, adjusted, compared with an untreated group, or tested. Only a tested claim says reduces or drives.
Provenance and what not to conclude go on the first page; read the assistant's prose as critically as its code.

quiz.concept: the provenance line shows which rows a result was measured on
quiz.q: The assistant sends a new draft of the churn report. The headline looks better than last week's, and the provenance line reads: 'Model trained on January to March. Headline result scored on all 12,000 advertisers, January to June.' What is the right read?
options: Too coarse: six months are pooled, so the headline should be split month by month
Stale: a model trained on January to March is too old to be scored on June rows
Not a test result: the headline now includes the model's own training rows
Too uncertain: it needs an interval before it can be compared with last week's
quiz.why: A result counts only on rows the model never saw, and half of those 12,000 are the rows it learned from, so the headline flatters it. An interval or a month-by-month cut would not repair that: a tight interval around a number measured on training rows is still the wrong number, and scoring later months is exactly what a test should do. The provenance line is what let you see it.

quiz.q: The assistant's draft says: 'Optimisation reviews hurt performance: reviewed accounts hit their CPA goal 25 points less often. Recommend scaling reviews back.' The numbers are computed correctly. Which rewrite can you stand behind?
options: 'Optimisation reviews may hurt performance: reviewed accounts hit goal 25 points less often.'
'After adjusting for size, tenure and vertical, reviews lower the goal-hit rate by 25 points.'
'Reviews cause a 25-point drop in goal-hit rate (1,798 reviewed accounts against 5,218 not reviewed).'
'Reviewed accounts hit goal 25 points less often. Observed only: reviews go to struggling accounts.'
quiz.why: This is an observed gap, and reviews are given to accounts already in trouble, so it cannot show what a review does; in this simulated world the review actually helps by about 9 points. Adding 'may' keeps the causal verb and only sounds careful, and adjusting for the visible columns neither moves this gap nor turns it into a tested effect.

quiz.concept: numbers bound to results, never typed
quiz.q: A creative-fatigue report drafted by an assistant says: 'Video creatives lose half their CTR 40 percent faster than static ones.' A join that double-counted impressions has since been fixed, and the chart under that sentence, regenerated, now shows a much smaller gap. The report goes out tomorrow. What do you ask for?
options: Every number in the text read from the results by the script, then a full reread
That one sentence corrected by hand, so that it matches the regenerated chart
The earlier chart restored, so that the text and the chart agree with each other
A footnote under the chart, saying that figures quoted in the text are approximate
quiz.why: The sentence was typed around an earlier run, so nothing ties it to the results, and if one number went stale after the join was fixed, others probably did too. Correcting it by hand repairs today's symptom and sets the same trap for the next rerun; the request is for bound numbers, checked row counts, and a reread of every sentence.

quiz.concept: one overall claim hides the segments
quiz.q: The assistant's segment section reads: 'Performance is consistent across account sizes: the ranking score is 0.840 for small accounts, 0.825 for medium and 0.851 for large.' The success team will work the 400 highest scores. What must be added before you sign that sentence?
options: An interval on each of the three scores, to confirm that the sizes really are tied
For each size: the share of churners on the list, and the dollars they carry
The overall ranking score, so that readers can see the three segments agree with it
The same three scores on the training months, to rule out memorising
quiz.why: A ranking score is measured inside each segment; it says nothing about how one list of 400 is shared out between them. Here that list catches about 55 percent of small churners and about 25 percent of large ones, while large accounts are two thirds of the spend lost. 'Consistent' is true of the score and false of the thing the team will use, and intervals on the three scores would only confirm a tie that is beside the point.

review.concept: the verb must match the evidence tier

variants.q: A guided bid-setup panel went live for every finance advertiser in March; no other vertical got it. Finance's goal-hit rate rose 7 points from the eight weeks before to the eight weeks after. Over the same weeks the other verticals rose 3 points, and the two had moved in step before the launch. Which sentence belongs in the report?
options: The panel raised finance's goal-hit rate by 7 points: the rate before launch against the rate after.
The panel is associated with a higher goal-hit rate in finance; no more can be said without an experiment.
Finance rose 4 points more than verticals without the panel, assuming both would have moved together.
The panel causes a 4-point lift in goal-hit rate, which the comparison with the other verticals has proved.
variants.why: The change in the group that got the panel, minus the change in a similar group that did not, is stronger evidence than an adjusted gap and weaker than an experiment, so the sentence reports the difference between the two changes and names the assumption it rests on. Seven points credits the panel with what the season did for everyone. 'Causes' and 'proved' claim a coin flip that never happened, and retreating to 'associated with' throws away what the comparison group bought.

variants.q: A pricing team offered a lower minimum budget to a randomly chosen half of new advertisers. First-month activation was 4 points higher in that half, with an interval from 1 to 7 points. The assistant writes: 'A lower minimum budget is associated with higher activation.' What is the right edit?
options: Keep it and add 'a test is needed': cautious wording is the safe choice for any finding
Strengthen it: the lower minimum raised activation by about 4 points (1 to 7)
Weaken it: with an interval that wide, the difference may well be due to chance
Rewrite it around the two activation rates to more decimals, and drop the interval
variants.why: A coin decided who got the lower minimum, so hidden differences between advertisers are balanced across the two halves: this is the tested tier, and the causal verb has been earned, as long as it travels with its interval. Hedging a tested result throws away what the experiment bought, and the interval already excludes zero. The test has been run, so asking for one is not caution.

variants.q: After adjusting for the background columns in the table, advertisers on automated bidding churn about 4 points less than the rest. No experiment was run. Which sentence matches the evidence?
options: After adjusting for what the table holds, a gap of about 4 points remains
Automated bidding lowers churn by 4 points, controlling for confounders
Automated bidding has no real effect, because the raw gap shrank when adjusted
Automated bidding is the main driver of retention among the practices
variants.why: Adjusting removes only the differences the table can see; a trait that sits in no column can still be behind the gap, so the claim stays one tier below tested. 'Controlling for confounders' sounds rigorous, but it promises that all of them were controlled, which no table can guarantee.

review.concept: a sentence that can be checked: count, baseline, interval, rows

variants.q: An assistant's report on a ticket-routing model says: 'The language model classifies tickets with excellent accuracy.' Which replacement could survive a question?
options: 'It reaches 96.0 percent accuracy across all six categories, well ahead of every other method tried.'
'I read 40 of its labels myself and found only one or two that I would have changed.'
'Of 450 unseen test tickets it got 432 right (interval 93.8 to 97.5 percent); keyword rules got 131.'
'The language model is highly accurate in most categories, and its few errors are on tangled tickets.'
variants.why: A count on named rows, an interval and a baseline on the same tickets can each be checked; adjectives cannot. A decimal place looks precise but adds no evidence: a bare percentage still hides how many tickets, which tickets, and how far ahead of what. Forty labels read by hand is a count, but too few to carry an interval worth having, and with nothing beside it.

variants.q: A report for finance says: 'The model forecasts daily platform spend very accurately.' Which version can you stand behind?
options: 'The model follows the last two years of daily spend almost exactly, weekends and holidays included.'
'Twelve forecasts from past dates forward missed by about 3 percent a day; same weekday last week, 6.'
'Across the full history the model's error averages about 3 percent, far better than any naive method.'
'The model includes trend, weekday and holiday effects, which is why its forecasts can be relied on.'
variants.why: It says how the error was measured, from past dates forward and twelve times over, and puts the naive method's number beside it, so a reader can check both the test and the size of the gain. Following history closely, or a low error across the full history, is a score on days the model has already seen, and 'far better than any naive method' names no bar.

variants.q: An invalid-traffic report says: 'The new detector catches bad traffic far better than the old threshold.' Which rewrite is the strongest?
options: 'The new detector flagged 60 publishers last month, against 35 for the old threshold: 71 percent more.'
'The new detector's scores separate normal and suspicious publishers far more sharply than before.'
'Three analysts reviewed 20 of the new detector's flags and judged every one of them convincing.'
'Of 50 planted incidents the detector caught 44 and the threshold 29, with 9 and 31 false alerts.'
variants.why: Planted incidents have a known answer, so catches and false alerts can be counted for both methods on the same cases: a count, a baseline and the rows. Flagging more publishers is not evidence of catching more bad traffic; without known cases it may simply be more false alarms.

drill.q: A report says that a practice reduces churn. Which four tiers of evidence do you check that verb against, and which one earns it?
drill.a: Observed, adjusted, compared with a similar untreated group, and tested. Only tested, where a coin decided who got the change, earns reduces or drives. Observed is associated with, adjusted remains after adjusting, and compared rose more than the comparison group, assuming the two would have moved together.

drill.q: After a rerun, the chart in a report changed but the sentence under it did not. What went wrong, and what do you ask for so it cannot happen again?
drill.a: The number in the sentence was typed instead of read from the results. Ask for every number in the text to be inserted by the script from the same results file as the charts, with a list of where each one came from.

recall.prompt: A colleague is about to send out a model report that an assistant drafted. In thirty seconds, tell them what to check before it goes.
recall.model_answer: Check that every number in the text is read from the computed results, not typed, and that each comparison shows its group sizes, an interval and the baseline, on rows the model never saw. Check the verbs: an observed gap is associated with, an adjusted gap remains after adjusting, a change set against an untreated group rose more than the comparison group, and only a tested effect reduces or drives. Make sure results are shown by segment, and that the first page carries a provenance line and a plain statement of what the reader should not conclude. Then read the prose as critically as the code: any sentence no number supports comes out.

ask_assistant: For every report you draft for me: build it only from [the results file we checked in earlier stages]. Insert every number in the text from that file by code, and append a table matching each number in the prose to its source. Beside every comparison print both group sizes and a 95 percent interval. Put [the baseline] next to the model on the same unseen rows at the same list size, and break headline results out by [segments]. Tag each finding observed, adjusted, compared with an untreated group, or tested; use causal verbs only for tested ones. Open with a provenance line ([pull date, rows in and out, model version]) and what the report does not show.
audit_checklist: A source table at the end: every number in the prose matched to the computed result it was read from, with none missing
Both group sizes and an interval beside every comparison, and the baseline beside every model result, on the same unseen rows and at the same list size
Every finding tagged observed, adjusted, compared with an untreated group, or tested; no causal verb on an untested one, and each compared one states its assumption
A first page that opens with the provenance line (pull date, rows in and out, model version) and what not to conclude, with headline results broken out by segment
transfer: A creative-fatigue analysis: 'video fatigues faster' needs the number of creatives in each group, an interval, and a verb that fits an observed gap.
A spend forecast for finance: the error measured from past dates forward, the naive method's error beside it, and a range on the first page instead of a single figure.
An invalid-traffic review of publishers: the count of confirmed or planted cases each method caught, its false alerts, and how many clicks each publisher's rate rests on.

other_ways.approach: A one-page decision memo instead of a full report
other_ways.when: When the reader has one decision to make. It holds fewer numbers, and every one of them still needs its source, baseline, interval and tier.

other_ways.approach: A live dashboard fed by the results tables
other_ways.when: When the numbers must stay current without a rerun. Binding comes free, but the evidence tier and the limits have to be written onto the page as fixed text.

other_ways.approach: A second reader briefed to attack the draft: a colleague, or a fresh assistant session
other_ways.when: When the report feeds an expensive decision. Ask for a list of every sentence that no number on the page supports.

glossary.def: A number in the text that the script inserts from the computed results, so it cannot disagree with the chart beside it.
Prose that still quotes an earlier run's number after the analysis was rerun.

How a claim was established: observed (two groups differ), adjusted (they still differ with the visible columns held fixed), compared (the change in a group that got something minus the change in a similar untreated group) or tested (a coin decided). It decides which verbs the sentence may use.
One line saying when the data was pulled, which rows were in and out, and which model version produced the results.
